Baird's sandpiper (Calidris bairdii) is a high-arctic breeding shorebird that exhibits a life-history strategy finely tuned to the short summer window of its tundra nesting grounds. Field studies on the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta have provided detailed demographic data for this species, with hatchling mass being a critical metric of early condition. Newly emerged chicks typically weigh approximately 6.1 grams [Wwb = approximately 6.1 grams], a modest initial mass that reflects the limited yolk reserves available at hatching in this precocial species. This low neonatal weight imposes a high energetic demand on brooded chicks, which must gain mass rapidly to achieve thermoregulatory independence. Data from growth curves indicate that mass gain is steep during the first week post-hatch, driven by high rates of parental provisioning. The adult body mass of females, by contrast, reaches a maximum of 38 grams [Wwi = 38 grams], representing a more than sixfold increase from birth weight. This ultimate mass is attained gradually over the course of the summer, with females typically achieving their peak body condition just prior to fall migration. Such a pronounced mass trajectory underscores the developmental challenge faced by a species nesting at latitudes where the growing season is severely compressed.

In controlled incubation experiments conducted at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, eggs of Calidris bairdii were maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] to simulate natural nest conditions. Under these thermal regimes, the age at birth, defined as the interval from oviposition to pipping, was recorded at exactly 20.5 days [ab = 20.5 days] at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This incubation period is consistent with values reported for other small-bodied Calidris species nesting in similar arctic environments, where ambient temperatures hover near freezing even during the breeding season. The precise thermal sensitivity of embryonic development in this species has not been fully characterized, but the 36 °C [T = 36 °C] incubation temperature used in this study is thought to represent the optimal maternal brood patch temperature for efficient yolk conversion. Hatchlings emerged with well-developed down and open eyes, already capable of limited locomotion and self-feeding within hours of leaving the nest cup. The synchrony of hatching within a clutch is typically high, with all four eggs usually pipping within a 12-hour window, a strategy that minimizes the period of heightened predation risk at the nest site.

Reproductive output in Baird's sandpiper is modest but consistent with its arctic life-history constraints. During the normal active metabolic period of the summer, when body temperatures are elevated to approximately 41 °C [T = 41 °C], females typically lay a single clutch of four eggs, although occasional clutches of three or five have been documented. The maximum reproduction rate can be expressed by considering clutch size and the number of nesting attempts per season. Females produce four eggs per clutch [N_R_i = four eggs per clutch], and in most years they raise a single brood per year [F_R_i = single brood per year], resulting in an annual output of four eggs per year [Ri = four eggs per year]. This low reproductive effort is typical of high-latitude scolopacids that face a severe time constraint on rearing young before the onset of winter. Clutch size in Calidris bairdii appears to be evolutionarily fixed at four, a number that balances the energetic demands of egg production against the need to minimize the time the nest is exposed to arctic foxes and jaegers. The 41 °C [T = 41 °C] body temperature typical of active foraging adults facilitates the rapid metabolic processing of insect prey, which is essential for maintaining the high provisioning rates required by the brood.

Developmental milestones in nestling Baird's sandpipers proceed rapidly under the thermal conditions typical of the arctic summer, during which active metabolic rates are supported by a body temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest territory, occurs approximately 18 days after hatching [tx = approximately 18 days after hatching], a value that falls squarely within the 16 to 20 day range reported for other small Ca at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]lidris species. This relatively rapid fledging period is critical for ensuring that young are independent and capable of migration before the tundra begins its rapid autumn senescence. Earlier in development, the time since birth at puberty, marking the onset of gonadal maturation, is estimated at 54 days after hatching [tp = 54 days after hatching], although actual reproductive maturity is delayed until the following breeding season at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This interval between fledging and puberty—approximately 36 days—represents a period of intense foraging and mass accumulation, as juveniles must build the fat reserves necessary to sustain a trans-hemispheric migration to South America. The achievement of flight capability and nest departure at 18 days after hatching [tx = 18 days after hatching] marks a critical transition that must occur before the tundra begins its rapid senescence at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C].

Longevity data for Calidris bairdii are relatively sparse, but comparative life-history modeling based on the closely related dunlin (Calidris alpina) provides a useful benchmark for understanding the species' potential lifespan. Under the active metabolic conditions typical of summer, when body temperature is maintained at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the maximum lifespan is estimated at approximately 28.8 years [am = approximately 28.8 years], a value assumed from dunlin records and representing one of the longer lifespans within the genus. This remarkable longevity is characteristic of arctic-breeding shorebirds, which often exhibit high adult survival rates offset by low annual reproductive output. Linked to this lifespan is the time since birth at first brood, which is estimated at 730 days after hatching [tR = 730 days after hatching], again based on extrapolations from Calidris alpina at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This two-year delay before first reproduction means that most Baird's sandpipers do not contribute to the next generation until their third calendar year, a common pattern in long-lived shorebirds. Such a delayed onset of breeding, combined with a yearly clutch of just four eggs [N_R_i = clutch of just four eggs], necessitates high adult survivorship to maintain stable population dynamics, a demographic strategy that is vulnerable to increases in adult mortality from anthropogenic or climatic perturbations.
